subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee Arabica vs. Robusta
description: A 60-second lesson on Coffee Arabica vs. Robusta.

hook.text: Two species dominate world coffee. Arabica is prized for flavor; robusta is prized for toughness.

buildup.text: Arabica evolved in Ethiopian highlands. It needs altitude, cool nights, and steady rainfall.

discovery.text: Robusta was found in Congo's lowland forests in 1898. It has twice the caffeine and resists more pests.

twist.text: Nearly all specialty coffee is arabica. But robusta makes up 40% of global production by volume.

climax.text: Climate change is pushing arabica to higher altitudes. Robusta may inherit the future of coffee.

punchline.text: Flavor vs. survival. Coffee's two species race ahead.

quiz.question: Which coffee species has roughly twice the caffeine?

details.summary: Arabica and robusta are the two dominant coffee species. Arabica accounts for about 60 percent of production and is prized for complex, nuanced flavors. Robusta, making up roughly 40 percent, is hardier and higher in caffeine but traditionally harsher in taste. Each serves different markets.
details.whyItMatters: The arabica-robusta divide shapes the entire coffee industry: pricing, farming practices, consumer preferences, and which regions can viably produce coffee.
takeaways: Arabica accounts for about 60 percent of global production
Robusta is hardier and has roughly twice the caffeine
The two species serve fundamentally different market segments

faq.question: Can you taste the difference between arabica and robusta?
faq.answer: Yes. Arabica typically has sweeter, more complex flavors with fruit and acid notes. Robusta tends toward earthy, woody, and bitter flavors with more body. However, well-processed robusta can taste clean and pleasant, while poorly processed arabica can taste harsh.

faq.question: Why is robusta used in espresso blends?
faq.answer: Robusta adds body, crema, and a caffeine kick to espresso. Italian espresso tradition often includes 10 to 40 percent robusta in blends. It contributes chocolate and nutty notes when well-roasted. Specialty markets increasingly experiment with high-quality robusta in blends.
